deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics: no formulas, numbers used in calculation, derivations or diagrams. It is a prose page of notes on ancient history, almost certainly taken from a lecture or textbook on universal history. The bundle label 'HB.Lagrange1816' does not match the content. The text continues the Diadochi narrative from fol. 156 and covers the following.

(1) The previous page ends 'Ptolemaeus kam auch, aber auf ein falsches'. This page completes the sentence: Ptolemy turned back to Egypt on a false report. Historically, Ptolemy withdrew from Syria on a false rumour that Antigonus had won.

(2) In spring 301 BC Lysimachus and Seleucus united their forces: 70,000 men and 480 elephants.

(3) Demetrius joined his father Antigonus at Ipsus in Phrygia. Antigonus presented his son to the army as his successor.

(4) At the battle of Ipsus, Demetrius routed the enemy cavalry but pursued too far. Seleucus then cut off his return with the elephants. Seleucus outflanked Antigonus's infantry, and Antigonus died at his post.

(5) The victors divided the empire: Lysimachus received all of Asia Minor ('Vorderasien'), Seleucus the rest.

(6) A new section heading follows: 'Dritter Zeitraum. Geschichte der einzelnen Reiche und Staaten, die aus der macedonischen Monarchie entstanden, seit der Schlacht bei Ipsus. 1. Geschichte des Syrischen Reichs unter den Seleuciden, 312–64 a.C.' The next page (fol. 158) duly begins with Seleucus Nicator.

There is nothing to restate in modern mathematical notation. The only figures are dates (301, 312, 64 BC) and troop numbers (70,000 men, 480 elephants).
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics.

Historical simplification: 'Lysimachus bekam ganz Vorderasien' is roughly right, as Lysimachus took Asia Minor up to the Taurus. However, Cassander's brother Pleistarchus briefly received Cilicia, and Ptolemy kept Coele-Syria in dispute. This is standard textbook compression, not a real error.

The figures 70,000 men and 480 elephants are broadly consistent with the ancient sources. Diodorus gives about 64,000 infantry plus 10,500 cavalry and 400 elephants on the allied side, and 480 elephants is the number traditionally ascribed to Seleucus's force. They are acceptable for lecture notes.
The Seleucid dates 312–64 BC are the conventional ones: from the Seleucid era to Pompey's annexation of Syria.

results.what: Lecture/reading notes on the battle of Ipsus (301 BC) and the partition of Alexander's empire; the heading opens a section on the Seleucid empire (312–64 BC).
results.modern_name: Hellenistic history: the Diadochi wars and the battle of Ipsus
results.usually_credited_to: Standard historiography (Diodorus, Plutarch's Life of Demetrius; 18th–19th-century universal-history textbooks such as those of Heeren and Schlözer)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely historical notes with no mathematical content; such student or reading notes are routine. Gauss's interest in history and languages is well known, and it is unclear whether this hand is even Gauss's.

checkable.asserts: The Seleucid period as dated in the heading (312 BC to 64 BC) spans 248 years.
The battle of Ipsus (301 BC) fell 11 years after the start of the Seleucid era (312 BC).

transcription_corrections: The first word, 'gemacht', is more plausibly 'Gerücht'. It completes the previous page's 'aber auf ein falsches [Gerücht]', which matches the historical account of Ptolemy's withdrawal. The following word ('Erscheinungen[?]') is uncertain; it is probably a verb of returning, e.g. 'wieder um'/'zurück', to give 'kehrte ... in/nach Aegypten'.
'Er stellte der Armee[?]': 'Armee' with a superscript mark appears correct.
'Er überflügelte Antigonus': the subject is Seleucus, continuing from the previous sentence.
The deletion of 'und' before 'bei Ipsus' and the correction 'auf'→'zu' are correctly recorded.
'Lysimachus' is written 'Lysi-/ma(ch)us' with 'ch' inserted above the line, as recorded.
